rule: Treat an acquisition offer as real only when it carries an expiration date or a term sheet promised within 24-48 hours and the acquirer applies time pressure; corporate-development interest without urgency is a vanity signal.

source.author: Justin Kan
source.work: The Founder's Guide to Selling Your Company
source.note: The original justinkan.com post (November 2014) returns 404; this is the archived copy of the author's 2016 republication.

rule: Once committed to a sale, share company data freely under an NDA so red flags surface before the term sheet, and refuse acquirer interviews of your team until it is signed.

source.author: Justin Kan
source.work: The Founder's Guide to Selling Your Company
source.note: The original justinkan.com post (November 2014) returns 404; this is the archived copy of the author's 2016 republication.

rule: Negotiate the business and legal points before signing the term sheet and push for the shortest closing you can get (target 30 days); after signing you cannot shop the deal and unsettled points default to the acquirer.

source.author: Justin Kan
source.work: The Founder's Guide to Selling Your Company
source.note: The original justinkan.com post (November 2014) returns 404; this is the archived copy of the author's 2016 republication.

rule: An acquisition happens when an internal champion at the buyer internalizes a strategic reason to own you; there is no right price, only the price you can negotiate, and the levers are willingness to walk away and a competitive bidding process.

source.author: Justin Kan
source.work: The Founder's Guide to Selling Your Company
source.note: The original justinkan.com post (November 2014) returns 404; this is the archived copy of the author's 2016 republication.

rule: Treat every investor as a no until they make a definite offer with no contingencies; if you believe one has committed, ask them to confirm it in writing, and count them as a no until they do.
Talk to investors in parallel, never serially, prioritized by expected value (how likely a yes, times how good that yes would be), and let investors who stall drop down the queue automatically.

A deal is not done until the money is in the bank: when an investor says yes, get the timetable for the money arriving and chase that process to completion, because even a day's delay can bring news that changes their mind.

State a fundraising target below what you hope for (say you are raising $250k when you would like $500k) so partial progress reads as momentum; reaching the stated number never stops you from raising more.

Sell no more than about 25% of the company in the seed-stage raise, on top of less than 15% earlier, because past roughly 40% sold a series A gets harder: VCs worry too little stock is left to keep the founders motivated.

Pick one founder, the CEO, to handle fundraising and insulate the others from the process, and keep growing during the raise: numbers that rise between two investor meetings make investors hot to close.

Give up a fraction n of the company only when the trade improves your average outcome enough that the (1 - n) share you keep is worth more than the whole company was before; the same 1/(1 - n) test applies to investors, hires, and advisors.

The time to raise money is when you can convince investors, not when you need it or when an artificial deadline arrives; first evaluate whether the startup is truly worth investing in, and if you cannot convince yourself, do not try to raise.
Treat fundraising as no more than plan A: write down precisely what you will do to survive if you cannot raise more money, and precisely when you will switch to that plan if plan A is not working.

Raise early money serially on convertible instruments instead of assembling a fixed-size round, giving investors who commit first lower effective valuations; rewarding first movers breaks the deadlock of investors waiting to see who else invests.

Size a seed raise as months of operation (usually 12 to 18) at roughly $15k all-in per employee per month, answer "how much are you raising?" as N months and therefore $X, and present plans for more than one amount raised.

source.author: Geoff Ralston
source.note: The library entry's URL (ycombinator.com/library/4A) renders the guide via JavaScript and serves no text to plain fetches; this YC blog URL carries the same work (January 2016) as server-rendered text.

rule: Prepare only a one-or-two-page executive summary and a walkthrough deck for a seed round, and treat an investor asking for detailed financials or heavy due diligence at this stage as one to avoid.

source.author: Geoff Ralston
source.note: The library entry's URL (ycombinator.com/library/4A) renders the guide via JavaScript and serves no text to plain fetches; this YC blog URL carries the same work (January 2016) as server-rendered text.

rule: Paper the seed round on well-known standard documents such as YC's safe, so negotiation reduces to one or two variables (the cap and any discount) and closing is as simple as exchanging signatures and executing a wire.

source.author: Geoff Ralston
source.note: The library entry's URL (ycombinator.com/library/4A) renders the guide via JavaScript and serves no text to plain fetches; this YC blog URL carries the same work (January 2016) as server-rendered text.

rule: Cold-email an early stage investor in three sentences: what you do in plain words, the one or two most impressive facts (market, launched product, growth, notable founders), and a specific ask; do not ask for a call or meeting, let the investor escalate.

source.author: Michael Seibel
source.work: How to Email Early Stage Investors

rule: Build the demo-day deck as roughly 5 to 7 slides carrying one idea each, legible from the back of the room; show each slide to a stranger, and if they cannot say the idea immediately, redo the slide.

source.author: Kevin Hale
source.work: How to Design a Better Pitch Deck

rule: Open the pitch by defining the company in a single declarative sentence of mission, not features, and answer "why now?"; the full outline runs problem, solution, why now, market, competition, business model, team, financials, vision.

Use a banker only when the company is late stage and selling on a multiple of profits or revenues; earlier acquisitions get bungled by bankers who push too hard on terms or upset the relationship between startup and acquirer.
Develop relationships with the acquirer's key people (corp dev, management, product and business unit leads) as early as possible, and research management's priorities before the first meeting.

Before signing a letter of intent, research how the acquirer has behaved between LOI and closing by asking investors, previously acquired startups, and startup law firms; that window is when the acquirer has all the leverage.
Move while acquirer interest is hot rather than waiting six months to hit another milestone; the fundamentals may improve, but the acquirer's interest can wane.

Learn the non-price deal-killer terms before negotiating (IP-indemnification clawbacks against investors are a non-starter for institutional investors) and hire an experienced startup law firm to catch them.

Engage acquirers only with a concrete reason to exit (exhaustion nothing fixes, a founding team about to blow up, an offer that pays substantially ahead of your likely value, a competitor about to crush you, or a real need for liquidity); otherwise stop the conversations, they are a distraction that usually leads nowhere.

Acquirers price companies on a ladder (team hire, team buy, technology buy, business asset, strategic asset) with higher multiples and more paid up front at each rung; pitch yourself a rung higher and find the acquirers whose strategy places you higher.

source.author: Elad Gil
source.work: M&A Ladder: Position Your Startup to Sell It for More

rule: Before accepting an acquisition offer, test whether selling 5 to 10% of your own shares in a secondary would be enough to de-stress your life; if with that money banked your experience, momentum, and gut say push on, do not sell the company.

source.author: Jason Lemkin
source.work: When Should You Sell Your Company?

rule: Once the startup has a real business and becomes an attractive acquisition target, pay the CEO at market, so the decision to keep or sell the company is not a direct response to the CEO's personal financial situation.

When employees ask whether you will sell the company, answer with the test instead of a dodge: if it achieves product-market fit in a very large market with an excellent chance of being number one it will likely remain independent, and otherwise it will likely be sold.

Put the Sean Ellis question (how would you feel if you could no longer use the product?) only to users who have experienced the core product at least twice in the last two weeks; results become directionally correct at around 40 respondents.

source.author: Rahul Vohra
source.work: How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product/Market Fit (First Round Review)

rule: Disregard feedback from users who would not be disappointed without the product, and split the somewhat-disappointed by whether your main benefit resonates with them: act only on the feedback of those for whom it does, because something small is holding them back.

source.author: Rahul Vohra
source.work: How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product/Market Fit (First Round Review)

rule: Build the roadmap half from doubling down on what very-disappointed users love and half from fixing what holds back the somewhat-disappointed who share your main benefit, stack-ranked by low/medium/high cost against low/medium/high impact.

source.author: Rahul Vohra
source.work: How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product/Market Fit (First Round Review)

rule: Keep surveying new users (no user twice) and track the very-disappointed percentage weekly, monthly, and quarterly as the product team's most important metric; expect the score to drop as you grow past forgiving early adopters.

source.author: Rahul Vohra
source.work: How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product/Market Fit (First Round Review)

rule: Treat product/market fit as reached only when you are overwhelmed with usage, often to the point of being unable to make major product changes; employee count and funding rounds are not fit signals, so until then stay lean and keep burn low.
Choose a market where users' problem is so dire they will try a half-baked, imperfect v1 (the hair-on-fire test: they would grab a brick, not just a hose), launch quickly, and listen to those users.

Define and test the value hypothesis first (what you will build, who is desperate for it, and the business model that delivers it), and move to the growth hypothesis only once the value hypothesis is proven.

First to market seldom matters; the long-term winner is almost always the first company to reach product/market fit, and once a company achieves it, dislodging it is extremely difficult even with a better or cheaper product.

Budget for market validation taking 2-3 times longer than you expect, and do not spend significant money on growth before fit: the Startup Genome study found 70% of startups scaled prematurely along some dimension.

Judge a consumer product's fit with numbers: DAU/MAU above 25% (over 50% is world-class), day-1 retention of at least 30% (over 70% is world-class), hundreds to thousands of organic signups per day, and scale on the order of 100,000 DAU.

Fix retention before spending on distribution: analyze it with cohorts, and hold off on partnerships and paid marketing while the bucket leaks, because growth activities cannot fix a product that is not working.

Rotate the priority as fit develops: earn satisfaction first by solving an urgent problem for three to five customers, shift to demand around 20 customers or $1M ARR, and get serious about efficiency (CAC payback under 18 months, LTV/CAC above 3) past $5M ARR; the climb to extreme fit usually takes two to six years.

Gauge your level of fit by how hard it is to find and serve the next marginal customer, and if stuck at the nascent level, get out with big changes to persona, problem, promise, or product: you are probably a 200% adjustment away, not a 10% one.
Look for problems you have yourself instead of trying to think up startup ideas: made-up ideas are doubly dangerous because they sound plausible enough to fool you into working on them.

Build something a small number of people want a large amount rather than something many want a little, and ask who wants this so much they will use a crappy version one made by a two-person startup they have never heard of; if you cannot answer, the idea is probably bad.

Get yourself to the leading edge of a rapidly changing field (a year is enough to reach an edge of programming), then notice what seems missing, turning off the filter of whether it could be a big company; that test comes later.

Turn off the schlep filter: seek the tedious, messy ideas others unconsciously shrink from (payments before Stripe), and make something unsexy that people will pay for; any sufficiently good idea carries as many schleps anyway.

Treat the initial idea as a starting point that will morph, not a brilliant stroke: a good-enough idea plus execution beats waiting (Google was roughly the 20th search engine), but spend at least a couple of weeks choosing it, and start from a problem, never a solution in search of a problem.

source.author: Jared Friedman
source.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript; the talk's transcript is carried in the page's embedded JSON.

rule: Score a startup idea by averaging four criteria: how big it could be (look for existing large companies doing something similar, or a small market with a real chance of being huge), founder/market fit, how sure you are the problem is big, and whether you hold a new, important insight.

source.author: Jared Friedman
source.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript; the talk's transcript is carried in the page's embedded JSON.

rule: Generate ideas from what your team is especially good at, the recipe behind about half of YC's most successful companies: for every company you have worked at, ask what you learned that others do not know, what seemed broken, and what was built in-house that other companies would need.

source.author: Jared Friedman
source.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript; the talk's transcript is carried in the page's embedded JSON.

rule: Differentiate real trends from fake ones: a real trend's new platform is used a lot by a small number of people, a fake one a little by a lot; pay attention whenever something is possible this year that was not possible last year, especially if next year will be too late.

Test an idea by whether you can articulate why most people think it is a bad idea while you understand what makes it good; the best ideas are fragile and sound silly, which is why they are still available.

Check founder/market fit before committing to a market: build it deliberately through test projects, working at relevant companies, or extensive research; make a brutally honest list of the abilities you lack; and pick a market you will still love as the product and market change over years.

Match the marketing channel to lifetime value: a product with a $10-15 LTV can only be grown with free organic channels, while paid advertising and content marketing need an LTV around $150 or more, which is what recurring revenue unlocks.

source.author: Rob Walling
source.work: The Stair Step Method of Bootstrapping

rule: Take the product to the nearest potential customer and build the venture from stakeholders who self-select by committing time, money, or resources; pre-commitments from key customers and suppliers reduce early uncertainty and substitute for detailed competitive analysis.

A university spin-out has little chance unless someone who did the original research leaves to run it full-time: do not recruit an outside CEO or wait for VC validation, and expect a year or more of full-time work funded by savings, grants, friends and family, or a small pre-seed before a VC round; waiting too long to leave is the far more common mistake.

source.author: Jared Friedman
source.work: How to spin your scientific research out of a university and into a startup
source.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript; the essay text is carried in the page's embedded JSON.

rule: Split spin-out equity to anticipate future contributions, not reward past research: full-time founders get equal or nearly equal stakes, and academic cofounders who stay at the university typically no more than 10%, hands-on meaning at least one day a week of active work with vesting tied to it.

source.author: Jared Friedman
source.work: How to spin your scientific research out of a university and into a startup
source.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript; the essay text is carried in the page's embedded JSON.

rule: In the tech-transfer license, hold the university to 3-5% equity (above 10% causes problems), royalties ideally zero and under 5% with a termination point, and milestone payments within a few percent of money raised; consider an option to license instead of a full license, start the conversation early, and do not wait for the agreement to start the company.

source.author: Jared Friedman
source.work: How to spin your scientific research out of a university and into a startup
source.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript; the essay text is carried in the page's embedded JSON.

rule: Distrust your instincts about startups but trust them about people: if a prospective cofounder, employee, investor, or acquirer seems slippery, bogus, or a jerk, do not ignore it; work with people you genuinely like and have known long enough to be sure.

Do not start a startup in college: it takes over your life, 20 is not the optimal age, and your early twenties are for breadth-first exploration; you are not sacrificing anything by waiting, because you are more likely to succeed later.

A startup is too much for one person, and all investors are more likely to fund you with a cofounder; if you lack one, getting one is more important than anything else: move to where people want to start startups, or switch to an idea people want to work on.

source.author: Paul Graham
source.work: Why to Not Not Start a Startup

rule: To get paid for creating wealth, put yourself where there is both measurement and leverage: a small group keeps your performance measurable, and inventing new technology gives your decisions a big effect, which is the combination a startup offers.

Decide by the worst case, not introspection about whether you are founder material: it takes at least a year without much or any salary to learn whether a startup is promising, so work out whether you can live with that outcome (counting what you would learn), because if you cannot, the anxiety will self-sabotage the attempt.

source.author: Harj Taggar
source.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript; the talk's transcript is carried in the page's embedded JSON.

rule: Judge a side project by depth of reaction: a single passionate user of a crude prototype hacked together in a weekend means more than a million waitlist signups; when a project and a collaborator who also wants to found energize you more than the day job, that is the time to jump.

source.author: Harj Taggar
source.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript; the talk's transcript is carried in the page's embedded JSON.

rule: Keep your life cheap and flexible so risk stays easy to take, look for small bets that lose 1x if wrong but pay 100x if right, then make a bigger bet in that direction; do not save up at a comfortable job too long, because lifestyles match next year's salary and the treadmill gets hard to leave.

You get truly rich by owning equity in things that increase rapidly in value, a piece of a business, real estate, or IP, not by selling your time, which scales linearly; the way to make things that grow that fast is making things people want at scale.

On venture funding, treat every month of growth below 20% as a red flag instead of excusing it with money in the bank or a nascent market: a stall means the current fit cannot justify the next round, and the market, not product shipping speed, sets most of the growth rate.

source.author: Sahil Lavingia
source.work: Reflecting on My Failure to Build a Billion-Dollar Company

rule: Evaluate what to work on by the utility delta over the current state of the art multiplied by the number of people affected: a big difference for a small group and a small difference for a vast number have roughly the same area under the curve.

source.author: Elon Musk
source.work: Elon Musk on How to Build the Future

rule: The founder stock split is set once and tends to be set in stone, and it is apportioned optimally when every founder feels they are getting a slightly bad deal, doing more than they should for the amount of stock they hold.

Get to ramen profitable, making just enough to pay the founders' living expenses: crossing that line changes your relationship with investors, is great for morale, and puts you back in control of your own destiny.

You make what you measure: put the number you want to grow on a big piece of paper on the wall and plot it every day, because merely measuring something tends to improve it, and be careful what you measure.

Do not suppress misgivings about a prospective cofounder: most founder disputes come from the people rather than the situation, and the founders burned by them usually had doubts they suppressed when the company started.

Raise enough to reach the next visibly higher level (an idea needs a working prototype, a prototype needs a launch, a launch needs significant growth), plus 50% to 100% more, because software takes longer to write and deals longer to close than you expect.

Take the first reasonable VC deal you get (a reputable firm, a reasonable valuation, no unusually onerous terms): startups are economically an all-or-nothing game, so bargain-hunting among investors wastes time you need for building.

Test a consumer idea by launching it and seeing what happens, and an enterprise idea by trying to sell it first: get a letter of intent from a customer saying they will buy before you write a line of code.

Set the cofounder equity split early (the conversation only gets harder with time) and split nearly equally; with two founders, give one person a single extra share to prevent deadlock if the cofounders fall out.

Build a product improvement engine: talk to users, watch them use the product, fix what is sub-par, and repeat (improving the product 5% every week compounds), and put no one between the founders and the users for as long as possible, so the founders do sales and support themselves.

With a paid product under roughly $500 customer lifetime value you generally cannot afford sales: experiment with acquisition channels (SEO/SEM, ads, mailings) and try to repay customer acquisition cost in 3 months; above $500 net LTV you can afford direct sales, and the founder sells first to learn what works.

Only think about how things will work at 10x your current scale and figure the rest out when you get there: far more startups die debating how to operate at massive scale than die from thinking about it too little.

Look for the 90/10 solution: the way to accomplish 90% of what you want with 10% of the work, which is almost always available if you search for it; a 90% solution to a real customer problem available now beats a 100% solution that takes ages to build.
Avoid long negotiated deals with large companies and corporate-development conversations: deals between large companies and tiny startups take too long, cost too much, and often fail completely.

You choose customers as much as they choose you: recruit 10 customers with a burning problem over 1,000 with a passing annoyance, and fire customers who cost more than they provide in revenue or learning, as Justin.tv did on the way to becoming Twitch.

Allocate equity widely: Sun's first founders together kept less than half the common (about 25 to 27%) with an equal or larger share for subsequent hires, and Khosla advises a founder to keep 15% and hire one or two magnet people at similar stakes, because the people you want compare your offer to starting their own company.

source.author: Vinod Khosla
source.work: Vinod Khosla on How to Build the Future

rule: To find a cofounder, list the people you know best who would be great, ask each directly over coffee, and when one declines, ask who their own top three or four picks would be and get introductions to them; repeat down the growing tree.

source.author: Harj Taggar
source.work: How to find the right co-founder
source.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript and serves no text to plain fetches; the talk's transcript was read from a Wayback Machine snapshot of this URL.

rule: De-risk a potential cofounder with a fixed trial: set aside one to three months full-time, or evenings and weekends, to build an MVP or pitch customers together, with an agreed honest keep-or-part conversation at the end.

source.author: Harj Taggar
source.work: How to find the right co-founder
source.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript and serves no text to plain fetches; the talk's transcript was read from a Wayback Machine snapshot of this URL.

rule: Before incorporating, agree the equity split (default 50/50, not docked for a few months of solo progress) and who is CEO; the title matters mainly to investors, who want one clear tiebreaker, and if both of you want it, you are not good cofounders for each other.

source.author: Harj Taggar
source.work: How to find the right co-founder
source.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript and serves no text to plain fetches; the talk's transcript was read from a Wayback Machine snapshot of this URL.

rule: The ideal founding team is two people with a history of working together, of similar age and financial standing, where one builds the product and one sells it; three founders is manageable, four is extremely unstable, and five works only when two dominate.

If you are going to fall out with a cofounder, do it early, recover the departing founder's equity into the option pool to keep the company going, and build in founder vesting as the pre-nup that keeps the breakup from getting messy.

Split founder equity equally or close to it: it takes 7 to 10 years to build a company of great value, so small variations in year one do not justify massively different splits in years 2 through 10, and investors read a 10% cofounder as someone the CEO does not value.

source.author: Michael Seibel
source.work: How to split equity among co-founders
source.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript and serves no text to plain fetches; the essay text was read from a Wayback Machine snapshot of this URL.

rule: Protect the split with the standard vesting schedule, four years with a one-year cliff: leaving within a year means walking away with nothing, the cliff vests 25%, and 1/48 of the total vests each month after; before a significant equity raise, have only the CEO hold a board seat.

source.author: Michael Seibel
source.work: How to split equity among co-founders
source.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript and serves no text to plain fetches; the essay text was read from a Wayback Machine snapshot of this URL.

rule: Size the option pool from a 12-month hiring plan instead of accepting the standard 20% of post-money ask: the summed grants usually come to about 10% with a CEO in place (15% if one must be hired), and in the worked example shrinking the pool from 20% to 10% raises the effective valuation from $6M to $7M.

Name the company in one or two syllables, abstract enough to survive a pivot, with one magical metaphor baked in; check the name against the USPTO trademark register, avoid sounding like famous startups, and plan to own the .com.

source.author: Jude Gomila
source.note: The original judegomila.com post no longer resolves; the Wayback snapshot is the reachable copy.

rule: File an 83(b) election within 30 days of the stock grant or early exercise: the IRS does not extend this deadline and missing it is essentially irrevocable, so mail it with documented proof of delivery and a self-addressed stamped envelope for the return receipt.

source.author: Holloway
source.work: The Holloway Guide to Equity Compensation
source.note: Holloway gates parts of the guide behind purchase; the cited mechanics are in the openly readable sections.

rule: Learn the post-termination exercise window before signing an offer, not after: expiration 90 days after leaving remains the norm, and options you cannot afford to exercise (including the taxes) within that window are effectively worthless.

source.author: Holloway
source.work: The Holloway Guide to Equity Compensation
source.note: Holloway gates parts of the guide behind purchase; the cited mechanics are in the openly readable sections.

rule: Fix time and budget and flex scope: scoping down forces real prioritization, and launching something great that is smaller than planned beats launching something mediocre and full of holes to hit a fixed time, budget, and scope window.

source.author: Jason Fried, David Heinemeier Hansson, and Matt Linderman
source.work: Getting Real: Fix Time and Budget, Flex Scope

rule: Meet every new feature request with no ('not now'): listen but do not act, and only when a request keeps coming back take the deeper look and start considering the feature for real.

source.author: Jason Fried, David Heinemeier Hansson, and Matt Linderman

rule: Keep no list of feature requests: read them, throw them away, and let customers be your memory, because the requests that matter keep coming back on their own; Basecamp's tracked request list was never consulted again.

source.author: Jason Fried, David Heinemeier Hansson, and Matt Linderman

rule: Make a solid core product the priority and scale later: Basecamp ran on a single server for its first year, and going from zero to millions of users forces a revisit of the design and architecture anyway.

source.author: Jason Fried, David Heinemeier Hansson, and Matt Linderman

rule: Shape work to an appetite instead of an estimate: fix the time at a small batch (one to two weeks for one designer and one or two programmers) or a big batch (six weeks) and let that budget constrain the design, because estimates start with a design and end with a number while appetites start with a number and end with a design.

Keep no central backlog: before each six-week cycle, hold a betting table over the handful of shaped, risk-reduced pitches from the last six weeks, and let unchosen pitches go untracked, because important ideas come back and an advocate can lobby again next cycle.

Learn a role yourself before you hire for it, and whenever possible have the candidate do a day or two of real work with you before hiring (nights or weekends work): for a developer, that means writing code on a real but non-critical project.

By at least a 10x margin, the best candidate sources are friends and friends of friends: go after the best ones relentlessly even if you think you cannot get them, because getting one person you want to join every five or ten tries is worth it.

Grant the first roughly 20 hires about double the equity your investors suggest: for a company on a good but not breakout trajectory, about 1.5% for the first engineer down to about 0.25% for the twentieth.

Have at least six people interview each candidate who gets hired, at least five of them peers rather than managers, and require each interviewer to file a binary hire or no-hire decision with a one-or-two-paragraph justification within 15 minutes of the interview's end.

Apply the keeper test to every position: if this person wanted to leave, would I fight to keep them, and knowing everything I know today, would I hire them again? If the answer is no, part ways quickly, and pay the people you keep personal top of market for the role and location.

Skip performance improvement plans: when technology or the company changes and a person's skills no longer fit, tell the truth, and offer a generous severance package, which once signed also sharply reduces the chance of a lawsuit.

source.author: Patty McCord
source.note: HBR serves only the article's summary to automated fetches; the full text was read from a Wayback Machine snapshot of this URL.

rule: Hire people who put the company's interests first and rely on logic and common sense instead of formal policies: 97% of employees will do the right thing, and most HR policy spend targets the other 3%; Netflix's result was untracked vacation for salaried staff and a five-word expense policy, act in Netflix's best interests.

source.author: Patty McCord
source.note: HBR serves only the article's summary to automated fetches; the full text was read from a Wayback Machine snapshot of this URL.

rule: A good product manager is the CEO of the product: full responsibility for its success, defining the target "what" rather than the "how", gathering information informally but never giving direction informally (crisp written and verbal communication), and creating leveragable collateral such as FAQs, presentations, and white papers.

Makers work in units of half a day at minimum, so a single meeting can blow a whole afternoon by breaking it into two pieces each too small to do anything hard in; batch meetings into office hours at the end of the working day.

Put everything on the calendar, including sleep and free-time blocks (the release valve that makes sustained full-tilt work possible), identify the directly responsible individual for every project, and let only the projects where you are the DRI onto your own calendar, tracking the rest in a separate check-in document.

source.author: Marc Andreessen
source.work: Marc Andreessen On Productivity, Scheduling, Reading Habits, Work, and More
source.note: Originally published on The Observer Effect, whose domain no longer resolves; this is the reachable a16z republication.

rule: Give every significant decision one informed captain who farms for dissent, seeking out different opinions at every level, before making the judgment call; after the decision, everyone including the dissenters disagrees then commits, and the captain reflects afterward on what worked and what did not.

Measure the growth rate of revenue (or active users as a proxy if you are not charging yet) every week: 5-7% a week is a good rate during YC, 10% is exceptional, and 1% is a sign you have not yet figured out what you are doing; 1% a week compounds to 1.7x a year while 5% compounds to 12.6x.
When anyone agrees to try your product, do a Collison installation: say "right then, give me your laptop" and set them up on the spot, instead of asking "will you try our beta?" and sending a link.

Every marketing channel's clickthrough decays as audiences develop immunity (the first banner ad, on HotWired in 1994, had a 78% clickthrough rate; Facebook banners in 2011 ran 0.05%): fresh creative and new publishers extend a channel's life, but the 10x move is discovering the next untapped channel before competitors saturate it.

Product-market fit is one of four fits a $100M-path company needs simultaneously: market-product, product-channel, channel-model, and model-market; because you do not control the channel's rules, products are molded to fit channels rather than the reverse, and a change in any one fit forces a revisit of the others.

source.author: Brian Balfour
source.work: Why Product Market Fit Isn't Enough

rule: A creator can make a living from roughly 1,000 true fans, people who will buy anything you produce, by earning on average $100 of profit from each per year and being paid directly, with no label, publisher, or retailer keeping the margin.

Seven strategies account for how the biggest consumer apps got their first 1,000 users; most succeeded with a single strategy and none used more than three, and the most popular ones go to target users directly, online, offline, and through friends, with the founders doing the recruiting personally.

source.author: Lenny Rachitsky
source.work: How the Biggest Consumer Apps Got Their First 1,000 Users

rule: Use the 10/5/20 rule: set a price your customer immediately understands to be a tenth of the value delivered, then practice raising prices by 5% at a time, and keep raising until you are losing 20% of your deals.

rule: Your price dictates your acquisition strategy: at $2,000 a year or less the product must be self-serve with inbound marketing, no sales team, and same-day conversion; between $2,000 and $10,000 you can add inside sales reps, demos, and a sales cycle of one to three months; over $25,000 is enterprise, with dedicated sales and six-to-twelve-month cycles; months-long closes at prices that cannot cover them are the danger zone.

rule: The cheapest customers generate the most support: in the worked tier ladder, the $9-a-month tier filed seven times the support requests per account of the $199 tier (the $29 tier four times, the $79 tier three times); price for free or price for dear, never price for cheap.

source.author: Patrick McKenzie with Ramit Sethi
source.work: Why Your Customers Would Be Happier If You Charged More

rule: For low-touch SaaS, default to three tiers at price points like $49/$99/$249 a month, offer annual billing at the same rates with one month free, keep the top tier even if it sells nothing at first, and revisit pricing quarterly instead of leaving it alone for years.

To build a $100 million revenue business you need one of: 1,000 enterprises paying $100k+ a year, 10,000 companies at $10k+, 100,000 small businesses at $1k+, 1 million consumers at $100+, or 10 million active users monetized at $10+ through ads; the $1k tier takes roughly 0.5-2 million trial signups and inbound marketing, the consumer tiers need virality, and the ad-supported tier needs a high viral coefficient or UGC-driven SEO.

source.author: Christoph Janz
source.work: Five Ways to Build a $100 Million Business

rule: Hire a VP of sales who has sold at a startup at your ARR today, or at most where you will be 12 months from now, and at your average deal size: someone who has only done $50,000+ deals has no idea how to manage a high-velocity inbound team doing $5,000 deals, and the 4 ARR stages x 2 competitive contexts x 3 deal sizes x 2 lead types make 48 distinct profiles to match.

source.author: Jason Lemkin
source.work: The 48 Types of VP Sales. Make Deadly Sure You Hire the Right One

rule: Find willingness to pay with four ranged questions per buyer persona (at what price is this way too expensive; getting expensive but still considered; a really good deal; so cheap you question the quality), sent as surveys of 3-5 questions every three weeks, which generate responses at four times the rate of longer quarterly surveys; the too-cheap answer sets your bottom limit.

source.author: Patrick Campbell
source.work: The Price Is Right: Essential Tips for Nailing Your Pricing Strategy (First Round Review)

rule: Judge customer interest by what the person actually does, not what they say they want to do: stack listening conversations with commitment signals such as time invested, usage data, and post-use follow-ups, because no single evidence source gives complete coverage.

source.author: Rob Fitzpatrick
source.work: Signal stacking for more comprehensive customer insights

rule: Use customer conversations to attack market risk (whether people want it and will adopt it) and in sales-led businesses where the meetings already happen; when the risk is product or execution feasibility, or the problem is murky and future-focused, conversations yield learning but not validation, so reach for a prototype or another test instead.

source.author: Rob Fitzpatrick
source.work: Customer convos are the carpenter's hammer // Pick the right tool for the job // Validation Quads v0.9

rule: Cap paid acquisition at 30-40 percent of top-of-funnel and build viral features, referral programs, and content/SEO alongside it, because paid channels get more expensive and harder to track as spend scales and payback periods stretch as campaigns run.

source.author: Andrew Chen
source.work: How Startups Die from Their Addiction to Paid Marketing

rule: Compute CAC as the full per-user cost of acquisition, including referral fees, credits, and discounts, and report paid CAC per channel separately from blended CAC, because blended numbers hide whether the paid acquisition budget can scale profitably.

source.author: Jeff Jordan, Anu Hariharan, Frank Chen, and Preethi Kasireddy

rule: Put an employee option plan of around 10-15% of the company in place at seed and Series A, and have it well-drafted before the fundraise, so closing the round is easier and faster.

Vest employee options over the typical 4 years with a 1 year cliff, on a linear schedule (standard practice in Australia) with a monthly vesting cadence after the cliff; keep vesting time-based, since performance-based vesting is uncommon at early-stage startups.

source.author: Dave Parfett and Ed Gregory
source.work: Crafting your ESOP: Key terms and best practice

rule: Leave the exit-strategy slide out of your pitch deck: a truly great business typically takes at least 7-8 years to build, a business like that creates its own exit options without planning for them, and investors backing the long game do not want you to have an exit strategy at all.

source.author: Samantha Wong
source.work: The Worst Slide In Your Pitch Deck
